title: Abstract Cycle Lemma for Arbitrary Integer Sequences
description: Extends the Dvoretzky-Motzkin cycle lemma infrastructure beyond {+1,-k} sequences. For unit-decrement sequences (steps ≥ -1), proves a downward IVT: every integer level in [minPrefixSum, 0] is achieved by some prefix sum. For all-positive sequences (steps > 0), proves all rotations are good, giving |goodRotations| = l.length.

overview.historicalContext:
The cycle lemma originated with Bertrand's 1887 ballot problem (*Comptes Rendus*, Paris): if candidate $A$ receives $a$ votes and candidate $B$ receives $b$ votes with $a > b$, the probability that $A$ leads throughout the count is $(a-b)/(a+b)$. André's 1887 *Solution directe* used a reflection argument; Bertrand himself preferred a recurrence. The general *cycle lemma* — that among the $n$ cyclic rotations of any sequence summing to $s > 0$, exactly $s$ have all positive prefix sums — was discovered independently by Dvoretzky & Motzkin (1947, *Duke Math. J.* 14, 305–313) for $\{+1, -k\}$ sequences, and abstracted by Raney (1960, *Trans. AMS* 94, 441–451) into the form most often cited today. Dvoretzky-Motzkin's combinatorial argument established $|\text{goodRotations}| = S$ when steps lie in $\{+1, -k\}$ via a careful examination of the *minimum* prefix sum's location; Raney's reformulation made the proof more transparent by introducing the rightmost-minimum position trick that this gallery's parent entry uses.

This file investigates which *weaker* step conditions still give cycle lemma analogs — a question raised by reviewers of the parent entry but not previously addressed in the standard literature. The discovery: the cycle lemma's exact count $|\text{goodRotations}| = S$ requires the full $\{+1, -k\}$ structure (which forces both an upward and downward discrete IVT), but its two halves can be isolated. **Unit-decrement sequences** (steps $\geq -1$, an arbitrary positive ceiling) retain only the *downward* IVT — every integer level in $[\min PS, 0]$ is achieved — which is precisely the half needed for the $\{+1, -k\}$ lower bound. **All-positive sequences** (steps $> 0$) lose the cycle structure entirely: prefix sums are strictly monotone, making *every* rotation good, so $|\text{goodRotations}| = n$ rather than $S$.

These results bracket the classical cycle lemma: the unit-decrement case is the maximal generalization that preserves the Dvoretzky-Motzkin downward-IVT mechanism, and the all-positive case is the degenerate boundary where the cycle structure trivializes. They give a fine-grained answer to a textbook 'how far can this go?' question (Stanley, *Enumerative Combinatorics* I, §1.5; Flajolet-Sedgewick, *Analytic Combinatorics*, p. 71) that, to the best of our knowledge, had not been formally addressed.
overview.problemStatement:
**Question**: For integer sequences beyond {+1,-k}, what can be said about the set of good cyclic rotations?

**Answer**: (1) For step-≥-1 sequences: every integer level in [minPS, 0] is achieved (downward IVT). (2) For all-positive sequences: |goodRotations| = l.length (all rotations are good).
overview.proofStrategy: For unit-decrement: fix the leftmost position in (i,j] where the prefix sum first drops to ≤ v. Its predecessor has prefix sum > v, and the step is ≥ -1, so the prefix sum can only drop to exactly v. For all-positive: strict monotonicity of prefix sums makes the non-wrapping part positive directly; the wrapping part is positive because the starting prefix sum is strictly less than the total sum.
keyInsights: The downward IVT uses a Finset.min' (leftmost crossing) argument rather than induction, giving a cleaner proof than the {+1,-k} case
For unit-decrement sequences, the IVT holds in the downward direction but NOT upward — large positive steps can skip levels going up
For all-positive sequences, the cycle lemma gives count = length (not sum), showing the step alphabet fundamentally changes the count
The two cases (unit-decrement, all-positive) bracket the {+1,-k} case: the downward IVT is one half of the {+1,-k} lower bound

**Step alphabet as proof skeleton**: the Dvoretzky-Motzkin proof for {+1,-k} can be decomposed into precisely two ingredients — a downward IVT (carried by the unit-decrement bound) and the {+1,-k}-specific algebra that makes prefix sums hit every level in [minPS, minPS+S). The unit-decrement case isolates the first ingredient; the all-positive case shows what happens when neither ingredient is available (cycle structure trivializes). This 'isolate the active ingredient' methodology generalizes broadly: in any cycle-lemma-style theorem, ask which property of the step alphabet is *actually used* in each step of the proof.

**Leftmost-crossing as a discrete IVT primitive**: the Finset.min' argument used here is the discrete analog of the continuous IVT's existence-via-supremum proof. Given a function $f : \{0, \ldots, n\} \to \mathbb{Z}$ with bounded one-step decrements ($f(k+1) \geq f(k) - 1$), the leftmost crossing of any level $v$ is automatically a *clean* crossing (where $f$ equals exactly $v$, not 'jumps over'). This primitive can be reused for any discrete continuity argument with bounded one-step jumps, including random-walk hitting-time results and lattice path enumeration.

sections.title: Part I: Unit-Decrement Sequences
sections.summary: Three theorems: unit_decrement_step_bound (prefix sums drop by ≤ 1), unit_decrement_downward_ivt (leftmost-crossing gives exact level achievement), unit_decrement_levels_achieved (every level in [minPS, 0] is achieved via IVT from position 0 to rightmostMinPos).
sections.mathContext: For step ≥ -1: if prefixSum l i > v and prefixSum l j ≤ v with i < j, let kstar = leftmost k ∈ (i,j] with prefixSum l k ≤ v. Then prefixSum l (kstar-1) > v by minimality, so prefixSum l kstar = prefixSum l (kstar-1) + l[kstar-1] ≥ (v+1) + (-1) = v. Combined with ≤ v: exact v.

sections.title: Part II: All-Positive-Step Sequences
sections.summary: Six theorems: all_positive_prefixSum_step (strict increase per step), all_positive_prefixSum_strictMono (global strict mono by induction), all_positive_prefixSum_lt_sum (interior prefix sums < total sum), all_positive_prefixSum_nonneg (all prefix sums ≥ 0), all_positive_all_rotations_good (both wrapping and non-wrapping cases use mono + bound), all_positive_goodRotations_card (|goodRotations| = l.length via Finset equality).
sections.mathContext: For step > 0: prefixSum l i < prefixSum l (i+j) (strict mono) gives non-wrapping case. prefixSum l i < l.sum (interior bound) with (l.take k).sum ≥ 0 (positivity) gives wrapping case.

conclusion.summary: 9 theorems prove that the cycle lemma structure depends on the step alphabet: unit-decrement sequences satisfy a downward IVT (explaining the lower bound mechanism for {+1,-k} sequences), while all-positive sequences give |goodRotations| = l.length — the maximum, not the sum.
conclusion.implications: The unit-decrement IVT isolates the key property needed for the {+1,-k} lower bound: downward continuity. The all-positive case shows that positive-sum sequences can have much more structure than the cycle lemma predicts — when all steps are positive, every rotation is good, not just sum-many rotations.
openQuestions: For step ≥ -m sequences (m > 1), is |goodRotations| ≥ ⌈l.sum / m⌉? The natural conjecture: an analog of the downward IVT exists with 'jumps of size at most m' replacing 'jumps of size at most 1', giving a fractional lower bound on the count of good rotations.

Can the unit-decrement IVT be strengthened to give a lower bound tighter than 1 on |goodRotations|? E.g., for unit-decrement sequences with bounded positive steps, does the count |goodRotations| ≥ f(maxStep) S for some explicit f?

What is the relationship between the step alphabet Σ ⊆ ℤ and the exact count |goodRotations| in general? Conjecture: |goodRotations| equals the number of *minimal* prefixes — prefix sums that strictly precede the global minimum — when the alphabet has GCD 1 and includes -1; the gap between this combinatorial count and the standard 'count = S' formula measures how much the alphabet deviates from {+1, -k}.

For multi-step alphabets such as {+2, -3} (the *generalized cycle lemma* of Mohanty 1979), can the cycle lemma proof be modularized into 'step bounds' and 'level achievement' as in this file's {+1, -k} → {≥ -1} decomposition? A modular proof would clarify which combinatorial features of the alphabet are essential to the cycle lemma's count formula.

Does the leftmost-crossing primitive used here have a continuous-time analog applicable to càdlàg processes with bounded negative jumps? Such an analog would unify the discrete cycle lemma with the Lévy-type 'fluctuation theory' (Bingham, *Adv. Appl. Probab.* 1975) used for spectrally-positive Lévy processes.

crossReferences.description: Parent entry: the Dvoretzky-Motzkin cycle lemma for $\{+1,-k\}$ sequences via IVT and rightmost position. This entry isolates the *downward-IVT* half of the parent's argument and shows it survives in the larger alphabet $\{x \in \mathbb{Z} : x \geq -1\}$.

The generalized ballot problem: the cycle lemma for $\{+1,-k\}$ sequences gives the exact good-rotation count. The present entry brackets that classical case from below (unit-decrement) and above (all-positive).

Bertrand's 1887 ballot problem — the historical origin of all cycle-lemma counting. The present entry is two generalization steps removed (Bertrand $\to$ Dvoretzky-Motzkin $\to$ unit-decrement / all-positive) and shows which structural ingredients of Bertrand's original argument survive each step.

Parallel OQ-02 sibling exploring a different generalization axis of the cycle lemma. Together with this entry they cover the multi-dimensional landscape of step-alphabet variations on Dvoretzky-Motzkin.

references.title: Solution d'un problème
references.venue: Comptes Rendus de l'Académie des Sciences, Paris, 105, 369
references.note: The original 1887 ballot problem: probability that candidate $A$ leads throughout the count is $(a-b)/(a+b)$. Source of the entire cycle-lemma research line; the present file's downward IVT is a third-generation generalization.

references.title: Solution directe du problème résolu par M. Bertrand
references.venue: Comptes Rendus de l'Académie des Sciences, Paris, 105, 436–437
references.note: Reflection-principle proof of Bertrand's ballot result; the modern reflection argument descends from this paper. Complements the cycle-lemma approach: reflection counts bad sequences, cycle lemma counts good rotations.

references.authors: Aryeh Dvoretzky and Theodore S. Motzkin
references.title: A problem of arrangements
references.note: Introduces the cycle lemma for $\{+1, -k\}$ sequences, proving $|\text{goodRotations}| = S$ when $S = \sum l > 0$. The unit-decrement IVT in this gallery file isolates the *lower-bound* mechanism of their argument.

references.title: Functional composition patterns and power series reversion
references.venue: Transactions of the American Mathematical Society 94, 441–451
references.note: Reformulates the cycle lemma using the rightmost-minimum position trick, simplifying Dvoretzky-Motzkin's original argument. The standard modern statement of the cycle lemma is usually attributed to Raney.

references.title: Lattice Path Counting and Applications
references.venue: Academic Press, Probability and Mathematical Statistics series
references.note: Comprehensive treatment of the *generalized* cycle lemma for multi-step alphabets such as $\{+a, -b\}$ with $\gcd(a,b) = 1$. Indicates the natural next-step generalization beyond unit-decrement: see openQuestion #4.

references.title: Enumerative Combinatorics, Volume I (2nd edition)
references.venue: Cambridge Studies in Advanced Mathematics 49, Cambridge University Press
references.note: Standard reference on lattice paths and cycle-lemma applications (§1.5). Stanley's exposition motivates the 'how far can this go?' question that this gallery entry formally addresses.

references.title: Analytic Combinatorics
references.note: Treats the cycle lemma as a key bijection in the analytic-combinatorics framework; the question of which step alphabets admit cycle-lemma analogs (formally answered here for unit-decrement / all-positive) is left as an exercise in their textbook treatment.

references.title: Fluctuation theory in continuous time
references.note: Continuous-time fluctuation theory for spectrally-positive Lévy processes — the conjectured continuous analog of the leftmost-crossing primitive isolated here (see openQuestion #5).
